title: Security and compliance: RBAC, Audit Logging, Data Residency & Secure SDLC controls and evidence workflows
author: Aisha Patel
body:
Summary:
This document consolidates Redwood Inference’s security and compliance controls, operational procedures, and evidence workflows across the following areas: RBAC and authentication, audit logging and log integrity, data residency and retention, secure SDLC requirements, incident response (security), compliance evidence collection, and risk/exception handling. It is intended for security engineers, platform owners, SREs, and compliance stakeholders responsible for implementation and evidence preparation.

Scope and applicability:
- Applies to all Redwood production services, private deployment packages, and control-plane systems that process customer data.
- Excludes transient developer sandboxes unless designated as customer-facing or attached to production data.
- Owners must map this guidance to customer-specific contracts and regional requirements (e.g., EU/UK data residency).

1) Roles, responsibilities, and owner model:
- Security (owner): maintain policy, perform periodic reviews, and run evidence collection for audits.
- Platform/Infra (owners): implement RBAC roles, logging hooks, and log forwarding.
- Eng teams (service owners): validate role assignments, maintain service-level retention configs, respond to incidents.
- Legal/Compliance: define retention minima and long-term archival for regulated customers.
- Access Review cadence: quarterly automated access review triggered by the Identity team with exceptions surfaced to the Risk Board.

2) RBAC & Authentication (principles and controls):
Principles:
- Least privilege by default; role-based grouping for common tasks; temporary elevation via short-lived sessions.
- Separation of duties for deployment vs. approval workflows.
- All privileged actions require MFA and are logged.

Role definitions (examples):
| Role | Scope | Primary permissions | Review cadence | Owner |
| Agent-admin | Global control plane | create/delete agents, manage keys | Quarterly | identity-team |
| Platform-operator | Infra projects | restart nodes, scale pools | Quarterly | eng-infra |
| App-developer | Service-level | deploy, read metrics (no secrets) | Quarterly | eng-teams |
| Security-analyst | Cross-service | read audit logs, open incidents | Quarterly | security |

Authentication and session management:
- SSO: All interactive access uses SAML/OIDC via corporate IdP (Okta).
- MFA: Required for all human access to prod systems (TOTP + hardware key for privileged roles).
- Service authentication: short-lived OIDC tokens (recommended TTL = 1 hour) and rotation of long-lived keys no older than 90 days.
- Privileged session elevation: implemented via Just-In-Time (JIT) access with approval recorded in the workflow system (confluence link to JIT runbook).

3) Audit logging: what, how, retention, and integrity
Logging scope (minimum):
- Authentication events: login, logout, MFA challenges, token issuance/revocation.
- Authorization events: role changes, policy updates, access grants/revocations.
- Administrative actions: deploys, configuration changes, key operations, secrets-store events.
- Data access events: read/write of customer-sensitive data stores, exports, and backups.
- System events: node creation/destruction, autoscaling events, and erroring requests where they may indicate misuse.

Retention and storage:
- Short-term hot logs: 90 days in the centralized ELK/Splunk for operational investigation.
- Medium-term archive: 1 year for standard audit logs (encrypted S3 buckets with access logs).
- Long-term retention: 7 years for compliance-required artifacts or as required by contract/legal hold.
- Retention table (by data type):
| Data type | Default retention | Compliance notes |
| Auth & AuthZ events | 1 year (archive), 90d hot | Increase to 7y for regulated customers |
| Customer data access logs | 1 year | Customer SLA may require different region/residency |
| Infrastructure telemetry | 90 days | Aggregated metrics retained as needed |

Log integrity and chain-of-custody:
- Logs are pushed to an append-only store with object versioning and bucket-level WORM where required.
- Hash chaining: daily digest of logs computed and stored in immutable artifacts (signed by the security team).
- Alerts for log delivery failure: PagerDuty alert on 5m sustained failure to deliver logs to the centralized pipeline.

Log forwarding and SIEM:
- Production logs are forwarded in near-real-time to the corporate SIEM for correlation and long-term storage.
- Alerting rules for suspicious access patterns (see Appendix A sample rules).

4) Data residency and retention controls:
- Region mapping: customer data must be stored in the customer-selected region(s) (e.g., us-west-2, eu-west-1) with strict routing and storage policies.
- Encryption at rest: AES-256 for storage; CMK via customer-managed KMS for Dedicated/Private customers where requested.
- Encryption in transit: TLS 1.2+ with strong ciphers, mutual TLS for internal service-to-service where required.
- Backup and snapshot policies: backups inherit the same residency and encryption rules.

Retention policy (high level):
- Customer transactional data: default retention per contract (30–365 days typical).
- Audit logs: see Audit logging table above.
- Backups: rolling daily snapshots retained 30 days; weekly archives for 1 year; monthly for 7 years when required.

Cross-border transfer controls:
- Transfers require legal review and must be logged; standard contractual clauses (SCC) used for EU transfers when applicable.
- Private deployments: if customer requires on-prem or VPC-only storage, configuration must ensure no telemetry leaves customer environment except as explicitly authorized.

5) Secure SDLC requirements (minimum controls):
- Code review: All production code changes require at least one approved reviewer (two for security-sensitive components).
- Static analysis: Automated SAST run on every PR; high/critical findings block merge.
- Dependency management: Weekly dependency scanning for known CVEs; critical patches triaged within 48 hours.
- Secrets detection: Pre-commit hooks and CI checks, with immediate rotation policy on detection.
- Build reproducibility: Artifacts are built in the CI pipeline with provenance metadata (build id, commit, signer).
- Release gating: Release checklist must include security checklist items (SAST status, infra drift check, canary plan, rollback procedure).

CI/CD checklist (example):
1. PR review complete (including security reviewer if tag present)
2. SAST and dependency scan cleared
3. Integration and e2e tests passed in staging
4. Canary plan defined (traffic %, duration)
5. Rollback steps documented and validated

6) Incident response (security) procedures (summary):
High-level steps:
1. Detection & Triage — Security or SRE receives alert; initial triage within 15 minutes.
2. Classification — Determine scope (confidentiality/integrity/availability) and impacted services.
3. Containment — Short-term containment measures (isolate nodes, revoke tokens, suspend code pipelines).
4. Eradication & Recovery — Remove root cause, patch, restore services from verified backups.
5. Post-incident Review — Postmortem and evidence preservation, SLA impact analysis, and follow-up tasks.

Forensic and evidence handling:
- Preserve volatile evidence: memory snapshots, container images, and network capture (pcap) stored in an evidence store with access logging.
- Chain-of-custody: every evidence item is recorded with who accessed it and why; evidence is hashed and hashes recorded in the case record.

Escalation and communication:
- PagerDuty: security-oncall paged for P1/P2 incidents.
- Customer communication: security and customer success own coordinated external messaging.
- Regulatory notification: follow legal guidance for breach notification windows (e.g., 72 hours for GDPR where applicable).

7) Compliance evidence workflows and owners:
Evidence types and owners:
- IAM & RBAC configs: owner = identity-team.
- Audit log extracts: owner = platform-logging.
- System architecture diagrams and data flow maps: owner = eng-architecture.
- SDLC artifacts (SAST reports, release checklists): owner = eng-developer-experience.
- Incident records and remediation tickets: owner = security.

Evidence collection process (recommended):
1. Audit request received by compliance inbox.
2. Security triages request and assigns evidence owners.
3. Owners collect artifacts into the evidence repository (immutable snapshot).
4. Evidence is verified and signed off by Security and Compliance.
5. Evidence delivered to auditors via secure share or portal; retention of evidence copies per legal requirement.

Automation & tool recommendations:
- Use automated evidence bundling (CI job that packages SAST reports, build metadata, and policy attestations).
- Maintain an evidence index with metadata: artifact id, owner, retention expiry, and audit tags.

8) Risk, exceptions, and compensating controls:
Exception request process:
- Submit exception request in the Risk Board tracker with: scope, rationale, duration, proposed compensating controls, and owner.
- Reviewers: security lead, infra lead, legal for data residency exceptions.
- Approval: time-boxed (max 90 days default) and requires scheduled re-evaluation.

Compensating controls examples:
- If full RBAC enforcement is not yet implemented for a legacy service: require network isolation (private subnet), strict ingress rules, and additional logging/monitoring.
- If log retention exceeds budget: apply tiered retention and aggregated indexing to preserve forensic capability while reducing hot storage costs.

Risk acceptance and monitoring:
- Approved exceptions recorded in the risk register with automated reminders for re-evaluation.
- High-risk exceptions include mandatory compensating alerts and weekly status reporting to Security.

Appendices:
Appendix A — Sample SIEM rules (brief):
- Multiple failed role elevation attempts > 5 within 10 minutes -> Alert P1.
- New service principal created outside change window -> Alert P2.

Appendix B — Example commands and snippets:
- Exporting audit logs (CLI example):
  aws s3 cp s3://redwood-prod-audit-logs/2026-03-04/ /tmp/audit/ --recursive
  sha256sum /tmp/audit/* > /tmp/audit-digest.txt

- Evidence bundling (CI snippet):
  tar -czf evidence-${BUILD_ID}.tar.gz reports/*.json build-metadata.yml && \
  ./sign-artifact --key /secrets/signing_key.pem evidence-${BUILD_ID}.tar.gz
